entries: Wanderer, your footsteps are / the road, and nothing more; / wanderer, there is no road, / the road is made by walking.
Antonio Machado, Proverbios y cantares XXIX, lines 1 to 4, Poesías completas (1917) (trans. Betty Jean Craige, 1978)
Poetry

Corrected: the poem first appeared in the Poesías completas of 1917, not in Campos de Castilla of 1912, and an unconfirmed page number is dropped. The wording is Betty Jean Craige's, who set these four lines out herself, credited to her Selected Poems of 1978.
The Way is like a wide road. It is not at all difficult to find. The trouble with people is simply that they do not look for it.
Mencius, Mencius, Book VI, Part B, 2 (trans. D. C. Lau, 1970)
Philosophy

Corrected: a fourth sentence was dropped. Lau's first three sentences are attested at VI.B.2, page 172 of the Penguin translation; the closing sentence about going home and finding teachers enough could not be found in his wording, so the card ends at the third.
Spring is the time of plans and projects.
Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina, Part Two, chapter 13 (trans. Constance Garnett, 1901)
Fiction

The roofs are shining from the rain, / The sparrows twitter as they fly, / And with a windy April grace / The little clouds go by. / Yet the back-yards are bare and brown / With only one unchanging tree— / I could not be so sure of Spring / Save that it sings in me.
Sara Teasdale, April, the whole poem, Rivers to the Sea (Macmillan, 1915)
Poetry
To-day I made the ascent of the highest mountain in this region, which is not improperly called Ventosum. My only motive was the wish to see what so great an elevation had to offer.
Petrarch, The Ascent of Mount Ventoux, Familiares IV.1, opening sentences (trans. James Harvey Robinson, 1898)
Correspondence

Yet often the mountain gives itself most completely when I have no destination, when I reach nowhere in particular, but have gone out merely to be with the mountain as one visits a friend with no intention but to be with him.
Nan Shepherd, The Living Mountain, chapter 2, The Recesses (Canongate, 2011), p. 15; first published 1977
Essay
When I woke up to-day and got up and dressed myself, I suddenly began to feel as if everything in this life was open to me, and that I knew how I must live.
Anton Chekhov, The Three Sisters, Act I (Irina) (trans. Julius West, 1916)
Drama
I awake light-hearted this morning of spring, / Everywhere round me the singing of birds— / But now I remember the night, the storm, / And I wonder how many blossoms were broken.
Meng Haoran, A Spring Morning, The Jade Mountain, p. 108 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)
Poetry

Corrected: the poem stands on page 108 of The Jade Mountain, not page 152; that number is the scan sequence of the Internet Archive copy, not the printed folio. The 1929 edition prints the poet as Mêng Hao-jan.

To study the buddha way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self. To forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things. When actualized by myriad things, your body and mind as well as the bodies and minds of others drop away.
Dōgen, Shōbōgenzō, Genjōkōan, section 4, Moon in a Dewdrop, p. 70 (trans. Robert Aitken and Kazuaki Tanahashi, 1985)
Philosophy

When I left Queen’s my future seemed to stretch out before me like a straight road. I thought I could see along it for many a milestone. Now there is a bend in it. I don’t know what lies around the bend, but I’m going to believe that the best does.
L. M. Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables, chapter XXXVIII, The Bend in the Road (L. C. Page, 1908) (Anne Shirley)
Fiction
But let us open our leaves like a flower, and be passive and receptive; budding patiently under the eye of Apollo and taking hints from every noble insect that favours us with a visit.
John Keats, letter to John Hamilton Reynolds, 19 February 1818, Letters, XXXVII, ed. Sidney Colvin (Macmillan, 1891)
Correspondence
I was brought up in a distant province which lies farther than the farthest end of the Eastern Road.
Lady Sarashina, The Sarashina Diary, the opening sentence (trans. Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi, 1920)
Diary

Released from ice are brook and river / By the quickening glance of the gracious Spring; / The colors of hope to the valley cling, / And weak old Winter himself must shiver, / Withdrawn to the mountains, a crownless king.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Faust, Part One, Before the City-Gate (Faust) (trans. Bayard Taylor, 1870)
Drama

The Tao is in the Passage rather than the Path. It is the spirit of Cosmic Change,—the eternal growth which returns upon itself to produce new forms. It recoils upon itself like the dragon, the beloved symbol of the Taoists. It folds and unfolds as do the clouds.
Okakura Kakuzō, The Book of Tea, ch. III, Taoism and Zennism (Fox, Duffield and Company, 1906)
Essay

I never saw daffodils so beautiful. They grew among the mossy stones about and above them; some rested their heads upon these stones, as on a pillow, for weariness; and the rest tossed and reeled and danced, and seemed as if they verily laughed with the wind, that blew upon them over the lake; they looked so gay, ever glancing, ever changing.
Dorothy Wordsworth, The Grasmere Journal, 15 April 1802, in Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth, ed. William Knight (Macmillan, 1897), p. 106
Diary

I put one foot forward and drew the other back. If in the morning I had a genuine longing to seek eternal life, by the evening the attack of a whole host of desires had reduced it to impotence. Worldly desires were striving to keep me by their chains just where I was, while the voice of faith was calling, ‘To the road! to the road! What is left of life is but little and the journey before you is long.’
Al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error, III.4, The Ways of Mysticism, pp. 56 to 57 (trans. W. Montgomery Watt, 1953)
Philosophy
Does the road wind up-hill all the way? / Yes, to the very end. / Will the day’s journey take the whole long day? / From morn to night, my friend.
Christina Rossetti, Up-Hill, lines 1 to 4, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862)
Poetry

One day, as he followed the course of a stream, he became unconscious of the distance he had travelled. All at once he came upon a grove of blossoming peach trees which lined either bank for hundreds of paces.
Tao Yuanming, Peach Blossom Spring, the second and third sentences (trans. Cyril Birch, 1965)
Fiction

Above all, do not lose your desire to walk: every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it.
Søren Kierkegaard, Letters and Documents, Letter 150, to Henriette Kierkegaard, 1847 (trans. Henrik Rosenmeier, 1978)
Correspondence
Climb Mount Fuji, / O snail, / but slowly, slowly.
Kobayashi Issa, ‘Climb Mount Fuji’, in The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa (trans. Robert Hass, 1994)
Poetry

Hedged: the Ecco page was not opened, so the punctuation rests on a faithful reprint of Robert Hass and confidence is medium. Blyth's older version reads O snail, climb Mount Fuji, but slowly, slowly, and the two renderings must never be blended.

Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts. There is symbolic as well as actual beauty in the migration of the birds, the ebb and flow of the tides, the folded bud ready for the spring. There is something infinitely healing in the repeated refrains of nature—the assurance that dawn comes after night, and spring after the winter.
Rachel Carson, The Sense of Wonder, the closing paragraph (Harper and Row, 1965)
Essay

Oh, to be in England / Now that April’s there, / And whoever wakes in England / Sees, some morning, unaware, / That the lowest boughs and the brush-wood sheaf / Round the elm-tree bole are in tiny leaf, / While the chaffinch sings on the orchard bough / In England—now!
Robert Browning, Home-Thoughts, from Abroad, lines 1 to 8, Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845); text: Poems (Chapman and Hall, 1849)
Poetry

Corrected: the wording now follows Browning's first collected Poems of 1849, verified in two scans. The reading who wakes was found only in a reprint of 1896, and no 1845 printing was opened; every other edition reads whoever.
And this our life, exempt from public haunt, / Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks, / Sermons in stones, and good in everything.
William Shakespeare, As You Like It, Act 2, scene 1, lines 15 to 17, Folger Shakespeare Library edition (Duke Senior)
Drama
Life is what we make of it. Travel is the traveller. What we see isn’t what we see but what we are.
Fernando Pessoa, The Book of Disquiet, ‘Travel? One need only exist to travel’, last lines (Bernardo Soares) (trans. Richard Zenith, 2001)
Diary

If the way which I have pointed out as leading to this result seems exceedingly hard, it may nevertheless be discovered. Needs must it be hard, since it is so seldom found. How would it be possible, if salvation were ready to our hand, and could without great labour be found, that it should be by almost all men neglected? But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part V, Proposition XLII, Note, the closing sentences (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
Philosophy

A subject to which few intellectuals ever give a thought is the right to be a vagrant, the freedom to wander. Yet vagrancy is deliverance, and life on the open road is the essence of freedom. To have the courage to smash the chains with which modern life has weighted us (under the pretext that it was offering us more liberty), then to take up the symbolic stick and bundle and get out!
Isabelle Eberhardt, Pencilled Notes, in The Oblivion Seekers (trans. Paul Bowles, 1975)
Essay

Corrected: Bowles has offering us more liberty, not giving us more liberty, and no comma before and get out. The page could not be checked against the City Lights book, so it is dropped. The French original is Le droit à l’errance in Pages d’Islam.
You see things; and you say ‘Why?’ But I dream things that never were; and I say ‘Why not?’
Bernard Shaw, Back to Methuselah, Part I, In the Beginning, Act I (1921) (The Serpent)
Drama
Yes, there is goal and meaning in our path - / but it’s the way that is the labour’s worth.
Karin Boye, In Motion, The Hearths (1927), lines 3 to 4 (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
Poetry
Hedged: the spaced mark after path follows the Karin Boye Society setting of McDuff's Complete Poems of 1994. The printed page was not opened, so that one mark is medium confidence.
Our battered suitcases were piled on the sidewalk again; we had longer ways to go. But no matter, the road is life.
Jack Kerouac, On the Road, Part Three, ch. 5, closing sentence (Sal Paradise)
Fiction
Live not for battles won. / Live not for the-end-of-the-song. / Live in the along.
Gwendolyn Brooks, Speech to the Young: Speech to the Progress-Toward, Blacks (1991), closing lines; first in Family Pictures (1970)
Poetry

unused.quote: Life shrinks or expands in proportion to one’s courage.
unused.source: Anaïs Nin, The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Volume Three: 1939 to 1944, the entry of June 1941, ed. Gunther Stuhlmann (1969)
unused.note: Verified. A courage line before it is a renewal line, so it goes to the month that is about courage.

unused.quote: And I’ve grasped some solid and useful things in drawing and in painting, more firmly than you think, my dear friend. But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.
unused.source: Vincent van Gogh, The Letters, no. 528, to Anthon van Rappard, Nuenen, 18 August 1885 (trans. Van Gogh Museum edition, 2009)
unused.note: Verified. A letter of counsel about learning by doing the thing you cannot do yet.

unused.quote: I often say, when I make these little observations, ‘Had Aristotle cooked, he would have written a great deal more.’
unused.source: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, The Answer, on the philosophies of the kitchen, p. 75 (trans. Electa Arenal and Amanda Powell, 1994)
unused.note: HEDGE. Page 75 was not opened; the wording follows Arenal and Powell as two scholars quote it, and a splice with Grossman cannot be ruled out. A second Sor Juana is already held for June, so this one goes to May.

unused.quote: All the same I’m not going to accept your kind invitation, for the time being at any rate. The reason is that my pink cactus is probably going to flower. It’s a very rare plant I’ve been given, and I’m told that in our climate it flowers only once every four years.
unused.source: Colette, Break of Day, the letter that opens the book, pp. 5 to 6 (Sido, the narrator’s mother) (trans. Enid McLeod, 1961)
unused.note: CORRECTED and re-verified: a comma after All the same restored. The printed page is lending restricted, so the punctuation is medium confidence. A flowering that is worth waiting for, which is hope more than renewal.

unused.quote: Wherefore my counsel is, that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil. Thus shall we live dear to one another and to the gods, both while remaining here and when, like conquerors in the games who go round to gather gifts, we receive our reward. And it shall be well with us both in this life and in the pilgrimage of a thousand years which we have been describing.
unused.source: Plato, The Republic, Book X, 621c to d, the closing lines (Socrates) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1888)
unused.note: CORRECTED: the translator year is 1888, Jowett's third edition, which is the setting whose page was read. The closing lines of the Republic, and about the soul that outlasts the road.

unused.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
unused.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 9, Of Vanity (trans. Charles Cotton, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)
unused.note: Verified. Another Montaigne is already held for May, so this goes on to the month of clear seeing.

unused.quote: Life is occupied in both perpetuating itself and in surpassing itself; if all it does is maintain itself, then living is only not dying, and human existence is indistinguishable from an absurd vegetation; a life justifies itself only if its effort to perpetuate itself is integrated into its surpassing and if this surpassing has no other limits than those which the subject assigns himself.
unused.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity, Part III, 2, Freedom and Liberation (trans. Bernard Frechtman, 1948)
unused.note: Verified. Long, and it argues rather than opens the day; it belongs with the month on living and dying.

unused.quote: Travellers who require that every nation should resemble their native country, had better stay at home.
unused.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, Letters Written During a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark, Letter V (J. Johnson, 1796)
unused.note: Verified. Counsel in the form of a rebuke, so it goes to the month of counsel.

unused.quote: Patience, patience, patience, is what the sea teaches. Patience and faith. One should lie empty, open, choiceless as a beach—waiting for a gift from the sea.
unused.source: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, Gift from the Sea, chapter 1, The Beach (Pantheon, 1955)
unused.note: Verified. It is a stillness line, not a road line.

unused.quote: To awaken quite alone in a strange town is one of the pleasantest sensations in the world. You are surrounded by adventure. You have no idea of what is in store for you, but you will, if you are wise and know the art of travel, let yourself go on the stream of the unknown and accept whatever comes in the spirit in which the gods may offer it.
unused.source: Freya Stark, Baghdad Sketches, In the Moslem Quarter, opening sentences, p. 17 (John Murray, 1937)
unused.note: Verified, and a waking line, which April already had four of. Held for the month of hope.

unused.quote: When the spirit swells my breast I love to roam leisurely among the green hills; or sometimes, sitting on the brink of the murmuring Missouri, I marvel at the great blue overhead.
unused.source: Zitkala-Ša, The Great Spirit, American Indian Stories, opening sentence (Hayworth Publishing House, 1921)
unused.note: Verified. The refuter called its fit for April honest rather than exact: it is a marvelling line, so it goes to the month of stillness.

unused.quote: May lily-dotted lakes delight your eye; / May shade-trees bid the heat of noonday cease; / May soft winds blow the lotus-pollen nigh; / May all your path be pleasantness and peace.
unused.source: Kālidāsa, Shakuntala, Act IV (Invisible beings) (trans. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
unused.note: Verified to the letter, and dropped on rule 2 alone: the refuter could find no standard reference entry for the stanza, and Shakuntala is not known by it. A blessing on someone setting out, so it is offered again in December.

unused.quote: I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.
unused.source: Li Bai, The Hard Road, closing couplet, The Jade Mountain, p. 70 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)
unused.note: Verified. One Bynner poem landed already and only one may stand in a month, and the hard road is a courage line.

unused.quote: The time that my journey takes is long and the way of it long. I came out on the chariot of the first gleam of light, and pursued my voyage through the wildernesses of worlds leaving my track on many a star and planet.
unused.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 12, opening two paragraphs (trans. the author, 1912)
unused.note: Verified. The long journey inward, which suits the month of stillness better than the month of setting out.

unused.quote: A little madness in the Spring / Is wholesome even for the King, / But God be with the Clown, / Who ponders this tremendous scene— / This whole experiment of green, / As if it were his own!
unused.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘A little madness in the Spring’, The Single Hound, poem XXXVIII (Little, Brown, 1914)
unused.note: CORRECTED: the poem is number XXXVIII in The Single Hound, which has no Part II; that division belongs to a website. Dickinson stands at two of three, and the spring months are the place to spend her last.

unused.quote: The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,— / No higher than the soul is high.
unused.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, Renascence, lines 203 to 206, Renascence and Other Poems (Mitchell Kennerley, 1917)
unused.note: Verified. A poem of being born again, kept whole for the month that is named for it.

unused.quote: And the miraculous comes so close / to the ruined, dirty houses— / something not known to anyone at all, / but wild in our breast for centuries.
unused.source: Anna Akhmatova, ‘Everything is plundered’, lines 9 to 12, Anno Domini MCMXXI (trans. Stanley Kunitz with Max Hayward, 1973)
unused.note: Verified at medium confidence. Another Akhmatova is already held for October, so this one goes to December.

unused.quote: I got out of bed / on two strong legs. / It might have been / otherwise. I ate / cereal, sweet / milk, ripe, flawless / peach. It might / have been otherwise.
unused.source: Jane Kenyon, Otherwise, lines 1 to 8, Otherwise: New and Selected Poems (Graywolf Press, 1996)
unused.note: Verified. A gratitude line and a mortality line at once, so it belongs to November.

unused.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
unused.note: Verified opening line, carried from January. Woolf's closing sentence of A Room of One's Own is already held for December, so this one goes to May.

unused.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
unused.source: Karin Boye, Yes, Of Course It Hurts, lines 1 and 2, För trädets skull (1935) (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
unused.note: Verified in McDuff. Held because April landed the other Boye, and one person may stand once a month; the pain of growth suits the month of courage.

unused.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things can not be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one’s lifetime.
unused.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, Conclusion (American Publishing Company, 1869)
unused.note: Verified in the 1869 first edition, p. 650, and the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 1. It argues against prejudice, so it goes to the month of justice.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: CORRECTED: the sentence is in The Return, Part II, not The Scot Abroad, and it is the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 36. April already carried four essays.

unused.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
unused.note: Verified with the two-word for ever. Tolkien's small hands is already held for September, so this goes to July.

unused.quote: You do not have to be good. / You do not have to walk on your knees / for a hundred miles through the desert repenting. / You only have to let the soft animal of your body / love what it loves.
unused.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, lines 1 to 5, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986), p. 14
unused.note: Verified against reprints crediting Dream Work, no comma before repenting. April landed eight poems and this one is about permission rather than the road.

unused.quote: Our life is March weather, savage and serene in one hour.
unused.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Representative Men, IV, Montaigne; or, the Skeptic (Phillips, Sampson and Company, 1850), p. 174
unused.note: Verified in the 1850 first edition, p. 174. It is about the inconstancy of moods, which is impermanence rather than renewal, and the March refuter named it the first to drop.

unused.quote: And we should consider every day lost on which we have not danced at least once.
unused.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Third Part, On Old and New Tablets, 23 (Zarathustra) (trans. Walter Kaufmann, 1954)
unused.note: Verified in Kaufmann, The Portable Nietzsche, p. 322. Nietzsche stands at two of three and his child at play is also held, so only one of the two can ever land; this is the better of them.

unused.quote: You can’t get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book I, chapter 2 (Jake Barnes)
unused.note: Verified, Jake to Robert Cohn. It corrects the traveller rather than sending him out, so it reads as a truth line and not an April line.
